title: The blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
hookLine: the Lord bless thee and keep thee: the priestly blessing still used at Mass

cards: Near the end of a Mass, the people stop speaking, and something is said over them. A hand goes up, and the room hears words it didn't earn and didn't ask for.
In the book of Numbers, God gives Moses three short lines for exactly this. They aren't a prayer for the people to memorize and recite. They're a blessing, spoken over someone, by someone else.
And on some Sundays, those three lines from the desert are still spoken over a Catholic congregation before it goes home.

teach.h: THIS IS HOW YOU SHALL BLESS.
teach.b: First, who gives it. God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people.

Then the words, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee. The Lord shew his face to thee, and have mercy on thee. The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace." Second, its shape.
In Hebrew, the first line has three words, the second five, the third seven.

It grows like a wave building, from keeping you safe, to looking at you with mercy, to peace, shalom, a word that reaches past quiet toward wholeness. Third, the face. Two of the three lines are about God's face.
To have someone's face shine on you, or turn toward you, is the picture of being seen with delight; a child looking for a parent in the crowd at a school play knows exactly what that means.
At the end God says: so they shall put my name on the people, and I will bless them. The priests speak; God does the blessing. Fourth, where Catholics hear it.

teach.h: AT MASS, AND IN FRANCIS'S HAND.
teach.b: On the first of January, the feast of Mary, Mother of God, it's the first reading at Mass. One of the solemn blessings a priest may give at the end of Mass in Ordinary Time uses its words.

Saint Francis of Assisi wrote it out by hand for his friend Brother Leo, and that parchment still survives in Assisi. And Jewish priests' descendants still give this blessing in synagogue, hands raised over the people.

how: The priestly blessing from Numbers 6 is read at Mass on January 1, the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, and some solemn blessings at the end of Mass use its words; some Catholic parents also trace a cross on their children's foreheads with a blessing.

o: a prayer the people say together to thank God
words spoken over people, asking God's favor on them
a priest's formal permission to leave Mass

games.q: what's inside the blessing — tap the pairs.
p: in two of the three lines

s: the blessing was first written for the Christian Mass
it comes from Numbers 6, given to Aaron and the priests. the Church still uses it.
in Hebrew the three lines grow from three words to five to seven
it builds like a wave, ending in peace.
Saint Francis wrote this blessing by hand for Brother Leo
the parchment still survives in Assisi.

games.q: you're Aaron. God has just given Moses words for you to say over the people. at the end, God explains who is actually doing the blessing. what does God say?
o: the priests bless, and that's enough.
they shall put my name on the people, and I will bless them.
the people must earn the blessing first.
games.why: the priests speak the words and place God's name on the people, but God says: I will bless them.

practice: Bring one person to mind, someone you love, someone struggling, maybe someone you find hard, and picture their face.

Then, if you're comfortable, say the blessing over them, silently or aloud: the Lord bless thee, and keep thee; the Lord show his face to thee, and have mercy on thee; the Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace.
If you don't pray, simply wish them those three things: safety, being seen with kindness, and peace.

wordCard.voice: The blessing. The priestly blessing of Numbers six: keeping, a shining face, mercy and peace. Still heard at Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: may he bless you. the first word of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord bless thee. Three lines, spoken over someone else. Until tomorrow.
